# **Rocks Matchup Guide \- By Tinnoy & Gonzo**

## **General Rocks Gameplan**

Regardless of the matchup, your goal is to develop on a curve. It is important to prioritise your curve over plays that might look higher value. Rocks is a strong deck, with a huge drawback, so if you find yourself low on Shiki/Newgate/Linlin, you will die with heaps of cards in hand.

**Cards usage** 

![Streusen](images/cards/OP17-050-Streusen.jpg)
![Don Marlon](images/cards/OP17-052-Don-Marlon.jpg)
![Miss Buckingham Stussy](images/cards/OP17-054.jpg)

**Streusen** is cheap and flexible  card selection, and helps fill gaps on curve. It is ideal to see him in the early turns to make sure we find the missing pieces of our curve, but also does work clearing weenies vs Enel or Mihawk (RIP).

**Marlon** is basically our premium play on 3 DON. It lets us trash either of our 0 cost events for leader ability, and then immediately recover it, deploying pressure while growing our hand size at little to no cost.

**Stussy** excels as a late game play, once we have a strong board, since it lets us negate 2 of our opponents swings, and then becomes a pseudo blocker for a third one. She is also great when deployed next to Newgate on our SEC Rocks turn, totalling to 9 DON and cheating the race. 

![Ganzui](images/cards/OP17-043-Ganzui.jpg)
![Kaido](images/cards/OP17-042-Kaido.jpg)
![Edward Newgate](images/cards/OP17-040.jpg)

**Ganzui** is our tech as a concession for Elbaph Luffy. Once Mihawk is out of the picture, chances are Luffy will be our worst enemy, and this buffing leader forces them to choose between swinging or playing on curve. Right after that, it  becomes a 7k swinger that is almost impossible to remove.

**Kaido** is more of an universal option. It’s a 4 drop that works wonders with a shiki on board, making sure we remove a body, without having to spend additional cards. Super helpful in the mirror, and can be leveraged vs Loki decks in late game. As a rule of thumb, always show counter cards, and whatever card you aim to discard for the leader ability, Shiki or Newgate. 

**Newgate** is the backbone of the deck when going second. He turns any card into a 3k counter for swings at our leader, but can also push aggressive lines if our opponent takes the early lives greedily. He also completely overloads your lethal options, and if there are 2 on board, you can easily push multiple 11 swings in a single turn.

![Captain John](images/cards/OP17-044.jpg)
![Kyo](images/cards/OP17-045.jpg)
![Gloriosa](images/cards/OP17-046.jpg)

**Captain John** is a very reliable way to protect our board. Against decks with the ability to reduce power, he acts as a 6k baseline, making sure our key bodies can survive the turn. Of course it’s half the combo with the Usopp event, but this will be less important once Mihawk ban comes into effect, as we will likely abandon the EB02 Event.

**Kyo** is just premium removal protection on a body that replaces itself. It’s pretty much pointless on matchups without access to removal, but it will still let us push through some easy swings, or help dig deeper in turns one and two. 

**Gloriosa** is the best tool we have for slowing down aggressive decks. Removing a threat and eating a swing gives us a good enough buffer to safely deploy our Newgates and Shikis later on. This is a key piece vs Sabo or BLuffy for the early game, and removing Yasopp also does wonders. Once we reach lategame, it can be used both as a defensive tool or a cheap way to remove a blocker (prime examples being yamato or borsalino) and go for a comfy lethal. . 


![Shiki](images/cards/OP17-048.jpg)
![Charlotte Linlin](images/cards/OP17-049.jpg)
![There's no Authority](images/cards/OP17-055-Authority.jpg)

**Shiki** is the key body of the deck. 9000 statline on a 7 cost is always reasonable, since both combat and cost based removal becomes awkward. But adding his ability to immediately challenge the board with rush and power reduction just completely shifts the rhythm of the game. He is also part of our defensive line, and gets extra points against brooks and other character restands. 

**Linlin** is basically a necessity when going first. Playing a good body on 5 that turns a brick in hand into a 1k gives us incredible value, but additionally grants us powerful card advantage. Most of the time, we will draw 2, helping us follow her up with shiki, but in some cases our opponent will instead give up their resources, making the game a lot more predictable, and our Shikis all the more powerful when contesting the board. 

**There's no Authority** is most of the time a 2k counter, but in some matchups, piling up multiple in hand will turn a bad position into an easy win. It works in both our Leader and the Secret Rocks, so keep an eye out for it as a way to cheat the race. 

![Rocks Pirates](images/cards/OP17-056-Rocks-Pirates.jpg)
![Rocks D. Xebec](images/cards/OP17-118-Rocks-D-Xebec.jpg)
![Jinbe](images/cards/OP14-049-Jinbe.jpg)

**Rocks pirates** follows the same pattern, in most games, it’s a natural 2k counter, but in other matchups just completely turns the tempo around. Being able to deal with 6 cost bodies sounds meager compared to Gloriosa, but when facing Kaido or RG Luffy, forcing them to waste a turn re-playing King or SEC Luffy can buy us enough time to push them out of the game, especially if we can repeat the play with a sizeable board at the ready.

**Secret Rocks** is our boss monster. It’s a huge body that also lets us go super wide. Always plan for him when you defend (or let go) of your board. Letting us play 2 more bodies with a total of 9 cost is great, but it means we cannot have more than 3 real bodies by the time we play him, or instead we will waste resources.

**Jinbe** is our best option for non Rocks pirates. It’s a huge body with rush that nets us card advantage and also pushes a 7 cost or less back to our opponent’s hand. Can either be the best finisher, or a backbreaking tempo play, when contesting the board.

### **Ideal curve going second**

**2 DON:** Kyo to cycle a card and set up removal protection

**4 DON:** Any 4 cost character: Captain John, Wang Zhi or Gloriosa depending on the match up

**6 DON:** Edward Newgate. He lets you spend cards to be both offensive and defensive

**8 DON:** Shiki. Setting up defenses while punishing rested bodies

**10 DON:** SEC Rocks, combined with either Newgate \+ Stussy or Shiki \+ Kyo. This brings up our guard point count to 3 per turn, and sets up an unstoppable clock.

There are other interesting combinations to play out with rocks, such as Linlin \+ Gloriosa, but in general, you want to prioritise newgate and shiki above all else. 

### **Ideal curve going first**

**3 DON:** Kyo \+ Swing 6k with Leader

**5 DON:** Charlotte Linlin

**7 DON:** Shiki

**9 DON:** Shiki again \- If running Usopp event, keep 2 don open

**10 Don:** SEC Rocks, combined with Newgate \+ Stussy. Going first, we have already dropped double shiki, so it is more important to drop newgate, so we get some defense against leader on leader swings as well.

In general, it's relatively important to reach the endgame of at least 3 life, which will give us safety when it comes to making the 10 cost plays. 

From that point onwards, our board is very hard to contest and intimidating, so there are opportunities to use reactive tools like Gloriosa, Stussy and Rocks Pirates to bide some time and just snowball the race in our favour. 

And if everything else fails, there is always the option of Captain John Combos to buy an extra turn. 

## **Decklists**

Not many of us will get the chance to play a relevant tournament before the Mihawk ban comes into effect, but it’s worth sharing the list, in case anyone has a Store championship, and does not want to just commit to dodging the matchup:

![][image1]

The flex slots for the list are Streusen and Buckin, but you should not run less than 4 total. I prefer having more 1k counters available, so Buckin took priority in my lists. You can also cut Captain John down to 3 copies, or get rid of the Usopp event, but the combo does come up relatively often in the current meta.

We are playing the full 4 copies of Captain John because the endgame does rely heavily on seeing him, and early game, we might need to either trash him for leader, or let him go after it's been rested or has attacked. It is also very useful if we can develop him on 4 DON vs either Robin or Mihawk, to grant us 1k extra counter for each swing, or force them to waste the turn by committing to an 8 swing.

Only running one Streusen because it effectively compacts the deck, so there is very little cost to running him. Enel is not as prevalent, and while it does help kill weenies vs Mihawk, Wang Zhi will cover the removal in the early game, so we’re just playing it as a nice card to see, but is not key to the gameplan. He is also the easiest card to replace in the list, if you want to diverge, start from here.

Before we talk about why there is a single Usopp event in the list, we need to go over the maths of it. It looks like 1 out of 50 cards is a very low chance to hit it for leader ability, but considering an average of 8 turns before the end of the game, this compounds greatly. With some concessions to simplify the calculation, the probability of whiffing comes down to the following, based on the number of non rocks cards:

* 1 Non rocks card: We will whiff 1 in 5 games
* 2 Non rocks card: We will whiff 1 in 3 games
* 4 Non rocks card: We will whiff 2 in 5 games

The cost of a whiff is effectively reducing hand size by one, rather than increasing it by one, when swinging with Leader, and while it might not always cost us the game, it will be critical to how we need to approach the follow up turns, and if the timing is early, will be devastating. 

We decided to stick to a single copy, since the chances are lower, but also gives us peace of mind once it makes its way into our hand. From that point, we no longer need to factor in the possibility of reducing our hand size, and the question on whether we can afford to use leader ability disappears. For this format, a single copy of the event will be enough to outlive double Lunas from the green Leader. We will play this after the first luna, and they will need to replay the luna. This should give us enough defense to keep a sizable board after that and close the game.

### **The world after banlist**

The departure of Mihawk opens the gate to many archetypes to pop back into the meta, and removes our need to run a playset of Wang Zhi. This is great, but can also lead us in different directions. Chances are the mirror and Enel will start off as the main decks to beat, so we can take different directions depending on who we want to target.

![][image2]

This first list is great for the mirror, but will require us to play a bit more cleanly against Enel. Jinbe does a lot of work in the mirror, but means we do not get to play with 100% Rocks cards, and this could backfire on grinder matchups, so be careful.

![][image3]

We can also go in the opposite direction, and prioritise playing the full rocks stack. This means we have guaranteed card advantage, so we can grind Enel without being scared on every Leader swing. The tradeoff is the fact that having no Jinbe will mean there are less power plays to make in the mirror, so we will need to play that as cleanly as possible. 

![][image4]

Finally, this list is built to leverage Streusen a bit more, and make sure we find the needed pieces for each matchup. Kaido and John shine in different games, so running 2 copies of each should be enough to consistently see them at the right time, provided we aggressively leverage our lovely 1 cost.  He also helps attenuate the non Rocks situation, so that in key turns, we have a way to at least delay the uncertainty of whiffing leader ability.

As you can see, plenty of options for the decklist have opened up, and as the formats develop, you might want to try some other options yourself. So let’s talk about the parts of the list that can be moved around:

- **Streusen** is the easiest card to cut, he helps a lot, but never plays a defining role. Just keep in mind that when cutting him, you might also want to need to up the count of your 2 ofs.   
- **Buckin** is a necessary evil, because it’s the only 1k we are allowed to run without risking our leader ability hit rate. Run 2 to 4 copies. If the list feels too bricky, just up the count.
- **Wang Zhi** is not on the list right now, but if Enel becomes more prominent, it might need to make a comeback
- **Jinbe** is mostly here for Mirror and the Rosinante matchup, but if the latter is not a key part of the meta, we can probably get away with not running him. 

As for what other cards we could be running, depending on the meta, right now there are two main suspects:

- **Ganzui** is the Rocks pirate we should keep an eye on. He helps a lot against the Black Luffy matchup. Becoming a 6k will force them to choose on whether to develop board or push life, and being a sticky body means they will always need to account for their swing. If Bluffy becomes popular, we will want to slot a couple of copies.   
- **Gravity Blade Raging** is always a blue card to consider running in mid game heavy metas. Rosinante is all the rage now that Mihawk is gone, and GUffy is on a break, and it is not an easy matchup. If it grows popular and we need some help, this might take our non-rocks spot

## **Mihawk Matchup**

This matchup is defined by their mid game, and stopping them from going double 6c Law is going to improve our chances severely. Respecting Mihawk is the main reason to play Wang Zhi as a 4 drop, while also being obviously helpful into Enel. He single handedly makes our going first game a lot more reliable in the matchup. If possible going second would still give us a better chance of winning

### **Going first**

**1 DON:** Pass or play Streusen if you have one available

**3 DON:** Play Kyo and Swing 6\. Play the Kyo first, to offer the chance for them to trigger a Luna on them. The matchup gets better if they don't see multiple Lunas, so any chance to let them trigger it is great in the early game.

**5 DON:** Swing 6k with Leader, and then play Wang Zhi to remove their 1c characters. This stops them from playing OP13 Law on curve, and means they will instead have to simply develop a 5c character. If all of their weenies are rested (due to You Are My Samurai), you can instead swing into them and drop a Linlin to get defense and a bigger body, but it is fairly unlikely.

**7 DON:** Play Shiki and leave it active. Next best play is Newgate, letting you swing, but it is fairly weaker. 

**9 DON:** Play Shiki, and swing into the board with both to attempt and clear it. You need to make sure you have built up enough counters to survive their Shanks turn, where they will get 5 Extra don to work with. If our shiki is still on board, this is also a good turn to do a double 4 drop play, either removing a 5 cost or setting up defense with John to make sure shiki will survive until our 10 cost. 

**10 DON:** Develop the board while defending your best bodies. 

From this point on, it is a game where we will try to outrun their chain of Lunas (with some shanks. We want to pressure life with 8k swings if possible, and it will essentially become a race. 

Both Yasopp and Oden negate our blockers, so it's important not to count on them for survival (given they only cost Mihawk 2 Don).

### **Going second**

**2 DON:** Develop Kyo. He will remain standing pretty much the whole game. 

**4 DON:** Play a 4 cost body. Captain John preferably

**6 DON:** Newgate, and swing 8k into life if they have gone down to 4 or 3 life. If they have not, just starve and pivot towards board. 

**8 DON:** Double 4 drop, Gloriosa \+ John (must be a John if the 4 drop wasn't a John) or double gloriosa. Block when they attack back to make board for 10c turn

**10 DON:** 10c \+ 7c \+ 2c. Rest and hit board with everything you can and clear as many bodies as possible. The optimal board would be Kyo, John, Newgate Shiki and 10c Rocks. Their turn will be 10 Shanks. 

They will hit 12k into John, so we shiki \+ double 2k, and counter all the 6k hits into John. It is fine to let him die to the last attack as long as Kyo survives. This means you will keep your Rocks alive to swing into shanks. 

From this point, the ideal situation is to chain a second SEC Rocks into Shiki (and possibly Kyo), kill the Shanks, and survive the following turn on 1 or 2 life. This will be enough of a buffer to outlast 2 Electrical Lunas, and once their characters are gone, we can clear the game in 2 turns without much trouble.

## **Robin matchup**

Banish is a very annoying keyword on any card you face, but it is extra problematic on a Leader. This means that as a general rule, you will be happy to give 1 card to counter the leader swing, and instead take whatever swing they throw at you with the board. You are happy to go down this path of taking regular swings until you go down to 2 life.

Even though Robin does get some explosiveness from playing first, we just prefer our curve going second, so always choose to go second if you win the dice roll.

### **Going first**

**1 DON:** Pass

**3 DON:** Swing 5 with the leader and play kyo. No need to develop stussy here. If running marlon, you can trash an event to play him and recover it. 

**5 DON:** Swing 5 with the leader and play Linlin.

**7 DON:** Develop Shiki. If they have a wide board, do not rest any of your characters, as you cannot defend over Sweet Generals. Only rest your board if you can guarantee shiki surviving the clap back.

**9 DON:** Same idea as in 7 DON. Develop another Shiki/Newgate and keep your board standing if you cannot guarantee their survival. It is also an option to double Gloriosa if you have enough targets on 5 cost or less.

The best target for gloriosa is Oven, followed by 5c Smoothie, and then Pudding or Daifuku. 

From this point on, you will struggle for board space, so always try to block with Gloriosa on the turn you play her, to make space for your 10c combos. 

You will want to develop SEC Rocks on 10, and then contest board while chipping away at life slowly. Robin has a lot of defensive options, so try to avoid a scenario where you are playing for lethal, and instead play for board and snowball the game out of their hands.

### **Going second**

**2 DON:** Play down Kyo

**4 DON:** Playing out Captain John will give us free defense if robin still wants to play on curve, and free counter otherwise. If they spend their turn swinging 8 at John, just let him die and enjoy the tempo swing in your favour. 

**6 DON:** Play newgate and swing for 5k. It is never worth your card to take a life here, you would rather stay with a healthier hand size to defend board, and take hand size away from Robin instead. 

**8 DON:** The two strongest options are either Shiki or the combo of Newgate \+ Kyo. As mentioned before, keep your board standing, unless you know you can survive if they play Sweet Generals next turn. 

**10 DON:** It's time for 10c Rocks, accompanied by either of the 9 cost combos here. From here we want to heavily contest their board, so Double Shiki will do a lot of work, and we want to prioritise that if possible. 

From this moment, we are again just playing for board, and navigating around their sweet general turns. We want to play the long game here, and contest board while we chip away at life. 

One of the most backbreaking plays is to remove their only Linlin. If they have rested it, a second shiki all but guarantees removing it (spending two cards from hand). And even if they follow it up with sweet generals, their small bodies will not be enough to contest ours on the clap back.

Some Robins will actively play to deck you out, and refuse to expose their board to attacks, beyond 1 or 2 bodies that are susceptible to gloriosa. Keep calm, but be sure to not let them get too healthy either, and try to represent enough aggressiveness to stop them from tapping out, and instead they are forced to choose between Linlin and Giant. 

If the game is going in this direction, it is imperative to keep an eye on your deck count, because you can absolutely die by running out of it.

## **Sabo matchup**

This is one of our most favourable matchups, but it can get a bit tricky, especially when they chain multiple Lokis. We want to take second when winning dice roll, and given their aggressive nature, mulligans are a key part of the game:

- Gloriosa on 4 is critical to slow down the game, otherwise, they can smother us easily.  
- Linlin on 5 is critical to winning when going first. She gives counter power and a good body to contest the board in the early game.   
- Kyo is a great early drop for setup, and it can swing into sabo when it has 4 or more life. But you will want him alive on your 5 don turn if you are playing a 4 drop.

It is not worth starving on the matchup, but we do not really want to push for life too much, as they can get surprisingly tanky once they play the giants. If they defend heavily, don’t worry about swinging tall. If we have a Newgate on board, never use its ability to attack their Leader, unless they are on 3 life or less. 

Also, something to take into account is the deck’s explosiveness. 8 cost luffy is a rushing 9k swing, and each Elbaph Straw hat is a 6k power once giants are in play. Once you reach 3 life or less, take your time calculating how you will defend into this line of play. And do not forget that they could use Brook to make you trash a card from hand.  

This is a matchup where you will need to proactively use Shiki, and sometimes Newgate, when attacking, rather than only defending. For this reason, it is important not to over commit on countering early. Feel free to take life on swings that require more than one card. Even if you are on just 2 life, their swings are predictable, so if you control the board, you should be able to mark the rhythm of the game, unless you end up with a tiny hand size. 

Once Sabo gets a wide board, most of the bodies are easy to kill, especially when using Shiki. Loki is the main exception here, so it’s important to identify how long you can outlive loki swings. When attacking their characters, always keep tabs on the number of Robins in trash. If they do not have any, try to remove the other straw hats, and when using gloriosa, Robin and Usopp should be on your hit list, before anyone else.

Newgate and Shiki are a must on board, so don’t be scared of keeping them standing if you cannot afford to defend them on the clap back. Don’t forget about Robin here, as she will very likely be making an appearance to make them smaller. 

Once we have a dominant board, Sabo will not be able to break our defenses unless they come up with some creative options. 

Ground death is their best way to beat our captain John defensive line, but this can be bypassed if we develop a second copy. 

They can also try and swing the tempo by killing our board with Gum-Gum Kong Gun. Of course Kyo is a key way to stop them from even trying, so keep one at the ready for turns when the Gun would disrupt the tempo.

Their gameplan is to end the game before we stabilise, so when using Kaido, be sure to show them counter cards, to avoid giving them any info about our bricks in hand.

### **Going first**

**3 DON:** Develop a Kyo if you can. Stussy will stop them from swinging the 2c on Saul lines, but you would actually prefer if they did, so it’s not a premier play here. 

**5 DON**: It is imperative to play Linlin on curve here. We need hand size, and extra 1k counters can do some work if they decide to play Loki on 6\. This means the minions will unexpectedly swing for 5, and you could get up to 3 swings your way, Otherwise, the counter effect might only come when they hit us a bit bigger.  

**7 DON:** Play your shiki. If you can keep it alive, swing with it, but remember to calculate for them playing robin (Specifically Docking Pirate Six into Robin from trash)

**9 DON:** This is our Newgate turn, ideally accompanied by a Stussy to put the brakes on their offensive. You can also play out a Kyo instead, to get some protection for Gum-Gum Kong Gun or extra Lokis.

From this point onwards, the goal is to drain their resources, and set up a race they cannot win. There might not be a good window to play 10 cost Rocks, but Newgate and Shiki pull enough weight to not miss him when going off curve. 

**Going second**

**2 DON:** Ideally we want to develop Kyo. He will be a good loki defensive tool, and could help us push life or board in certain stops. 

**4 DON:**  Gloriosa removing the 2 cost they just played will swing the tempo, and let us swing face with Kyo and Leader. If we don’t find her, any of the 4/6 bodies is also decent to have on board. 

**6 DON:** As usual, we just want to drop the Newgate. As said above, only use him offensively if they are already at 3 or less life. Otherwise, a simple 5 swing with the leader will do.

**8 DON**: Shiki time\! Same as usual, swinging with him is fine, but don’t feel bad leaving him standing if he cannot survive a robin turn. 

**10 DON:** Secret Rocks into Gloriosa \+ Wang or Kaido. Setting up a wall while Newgate and Shiki are on board will be enough to become the aggressor here. Linlin can also be a fine option to accompany the blocker with. 

As extra advice here, there might be some tough choices to make with Kyo, once they play out Loki. Normally, it’s okay to let him go, and only defend him if you intend to play a 4 cost next turn, and you cannot afford for it to be loki’d. If they spend their mid game playing Gum-Gum Kong Gun, they are giving us more time for the Secret Rocks plays, and they cannot kill Shiki, so no need to keep Kyo around.

## Elbaph Luffy matchup

> Note: We are still working on this section, expect an update next week
   
This is likely the matchup where it matters the most to go second. Their curve is very natural on second, and they can easily drop multiple Lokis to break the race’s balance, while also making Shiki's power reduction a lot less relevant. 

Unfortunately, there are not many ways to make our first options better when going first. However, if you want to do so, Ganzui is your best friend. This 5 cost 7k character does two things that make the gameplay very annoying for Elbuffy. Firstly, it turns our leader into a 6k, so that they need to choose between pressuring our life or developing their board. And secondly, he is a very hard to remove attacker with a great statline. His ability lets us trash 2 cards to save him from being removed from the field, and that includes combat, so even through Robin reduction, the cost to keep him on board is fairly reasonable. 

The gameplan here is to defend early to stay healthy, because their Luffy chains are going to be a lot harder to defend. We don’t mind playing on low resources as long as they are in the same spot. And our Linlins do shine a bit more here than with sabo, because their Strawhats do not get buffed beyond 5k, so the countering part gains a lot of traction.

Unlike with Sabo, Luffy has a lot of ways to wall up on the lategame, so a lot of the endgames will go through one or two copies to the Authority event. If they go down to 1 life and we have established a Rocks, going unblockable on SEC and Leader lets you go 12/13 for a great chance at lethal. You might also have chances to map a 2 turn lethal if you don’t waste your copies, so be sure to leverage them properly, and consider the option to use Marlon to recover extra ones. 

## **Enel matchup**

This matchup does change quite a bit depending on the version, but the main assumption for now is the fact they are running a bunch of Dogs (Holy). This card is a 4k power 3k that brings double attack to both himself and all the Ohms, while simultaneously making those same characters 6k on defense. Combined with the army of pawns (1c 2k bodies that replace themselves), and its leader ability, it does pressure a lot while leveraging his events to remove whatever is causing him trouble.

These lists also pile somewhat heavily on ST-10 Trafalgar Law (and sometimes OP17 X.Drake) to drain their opponents hand size at random, making it hard to pivot the game, especially if our key card gets ripped off our hand.

This is also one of the only matchups where we would rather go first, since their aggressiveness gets miles worse when they get to swing first (and use their leader ability earlier). 

Gloriosa is definitely the card we want to see in our mulligans, as it’s a clean response to the block that will either force them to use a removal spell, or will double down as a buffer for a swing. If given the option, just block immediately here, because not doing so could backfire spectacularly if they Thor us for a bigger follow up swing. Of course if Wang Zhi is on the list, he can turn the game around if dropped mid game, so keep him in mind.

Enel is an extremely flexible deck, but it lacks real card advantage, beyond its pawns and RP Law. Fortunately, that is our strong suit, so if we can bring the game to go longer while we keep somewhat healthy, things will turn in our favor.

However, it is a very technical matchup, and there is no set desired curve, we just want to be reactive and leverage our extra resources, while we avoid dying to their crafty swings.

Our goal here is to always remove their 5k+ bodies, prioritising that over swinging face, forcing them to run on lower resources, and then stopping their 5 to 7 swings when we can afford to. Streusen will do some work on the clap back, but generally, it might not be worth swinging at the weenies, unless they have already used multiple shuras, and we can remove all of them in the same turn.

Weirdly enough, in this matchup, Newgate is fairly bad, unless we know they are running out of Gamma Knife. He is a prime target for the dreaded Gamma Thor combo, and even if it has replaced itself, the tempo swing of him dying is horrible, so only drop him on a curve if we have enough kyo security to not fall into this trap.

His long term plan of dropping SEC Enels is less common these days, but is also not great in the matchup, because of our Stussys freezing a base cost 6 (those Varies are all but useless). 

Shiki is the best card in the matchup. Shocking, right? His huge statline makes it awkward to remove through El Thor, and even in combat, can be a pain to deal with after a Gamma Knife. (since his ability reduces a swing by 3k, they need to commit a bit harder). He is also great at dealing with the SEC Enel, given it immediately turns it down to a 7k, and swings 9 at it, draining our opponents hand size by 2 at least (or one \+ mama).
Enel is very good at surprise lethals, so always keep into account how many El Thors they have left, and be aware that your 10c bodies might not even reach the ground. Feel free to counter with those rocks early, since it’s all but impossible to play more than one in the game. 

The general goal here is to arrive at 10 DON healthy enough to drop a Rocks, and clear their board. Then we don’t die to a greedy lethal, and we can set up a 1 or two turn clock to kill them while they struggle to develop.

There will be no ideal curve section for this matchup, because you need to be reactive during the early game, and their tools to disrupt your hand will make it harder to plan ahead a couple of turns. Just play to your advantages, and stick to your reactive plan. Linlin is a good tool to widen the card advantage gap, but in general you always prefer to remove their 5k+ bodies. 

## **Rocks Mirror**

You prefer going second, since your curve is more natural, but fortunately dice roll will not make a huge difference for the mirror. The first one dropping Secret Rocks will hold the initiative, but the real MVP is, once again, Shiki. The fight for board is a very natural part of the match, and Shiki lets us use our hand size in both offense and defense, by either clearing the board or bringing efficient countering when our board is attacked. Double shiki pretty much guarantees killing 1 or two rested bodies, or a lot of resources if there is commitment to defend them. 

Jinbe is the tech card of choice to make the mirror better, partially because it’s a very easy way to both contest board and bounce a shiki, both taking tempo away and lowering our opponents defenses that turn (since they can no longer use his ability to turn a brick into \-3k). 

There will be some stalemates, and Gloriosa has some very decent targets, with Linlin being the most obvious one, but Stussy and Captain John are great hits as well. Of course Kyo stopping the removal is annoying, but it still costs 2 cards from hand. This means that once he is on board, double gloriosa turns impact the resource war very heavily. 

On your 9 don turn, you might be tempted to set up the second shiki, but Newgate accompanied by a 3 cost will have a bigger impact in most games. Especially when you don’t have multiple rested bodies to deal with. 

As you will probably know, this deck excels at setting up tall bodies, and by the endgame, is very natural to have the trifecta of Newgate, Shiki and Rocks on board. This means that in the late game, when both of you have the big boys out, Stussy starts to shine like a diamond. For 6 don, you get to freeze both newgate and rocks, and every turn thereafter, you get to stop the most troublesome attacker, unless she gets removed herself. Meaning she doubles up as a pseudo-blocker, because they have to kill her. Beware of trashing them early, because you will definitely miss them by the end of the game. 

Missing your curve is a huge problem on the mirror match, and can get severely punished fairly quickly. Every resource counts, and not getting them at the right time will be pivotal. It’s both important that you see your pieces, and that you identify when your opponent misses them, as this will give you information on what they’re missing, and also let you punish it and get closer to the win. 

### **Going first**

The ideal hand you're looking for here is basically Kyo \+ Linlin. If running Streusen, he will help you get closer to those two, so value him highly. Of course a Shiki to complement them is great, but you should mulligan if you don’t see 2 out of the three, and some decent backup play for the turn you’re missing.

- **3 DON:**  Play the Kyo and swing 6k your Leader. Kyo is a key protection piece here when going first, so unless you’re missing Linlin, trash two cards to protect him from Gloriosa.   
- **5 DON:** If Kyo is still at the ready, develop  Linlin. She’s your best play this turn, but you cannot afford to get her Gloriosa’d on your opponent’s 6 turn. If you did not have kyo on 2, just develop Captain John or another 2 cost. IF you run him, Ganzui is not bad here either, as it can survive Gloriosa.   
- **7 DON:** As usual, play the Shiki, but he won’t have a meaningful swing target, so it’s not worth exposing to our opponent’s shiki. Just leave him standing.   
- **9 DON:** If your opponent also parked a Shiki, you have officially started a Shiki war, and you can match it with your second copy, leading to a fairly stalemated board. If they instead dropped a newgate on 8, your best play is to go Newgate \+ Stussy, freezing their Whitebeard. This also means there is no risk of double shiki from our opponent, so it’s time to turn the board sideways and pressure them.   
- **10 DON:** Rocks \+ Shiki is the best option, this gives us the hardest to kill body in the deck and an easy way to clear their board with Shiki. 

During the game, knowing when to swing our characters is going to be the most awkward thing to figure out. You need to start every turn thinking whether you can afford to attack with your characters, always assuming they will play a Shiki on the way back. If you have positive ways to defend that play, go for it. There will be a lot of turns where the leaders are just hitting each other, and with Newgate on board, there’s little point in going above 5, so take it slow and steady. 

Also, as said before, Stussy is an insane tool to stall the board on the late game, so be sure to accumulate them to leverage once the Shikis and Rocks are on board. 

### **Going second**

For the mulligan here, we are looking for some slightly different pieces. The best possible hand is Kyo, 2x Gloriosa, Newgate and SEC Rocks, but this is obviously not an easy one to pull out of the blue. You will not have many windows for Streusen going second, so he is not a great replacement, at least for Kyo and Gloriosa. Keep hands that could let you go back to back gloriosas, and even though SEC is great to see early, you have time to find him, so value him lower than the rest. 

- **2 DON:** Play Kyo to draw a card and set up some protection  
- **4 DON:**  Gloriosa whatever they played on 3\. If it was Kyo, they should defend it by trashing 2 cards. If they do and follow up with Linlin, consider trashing 2 to keep both on low count. They could miss shiki, so  if your hand is strong, you will push ahead.  
- **6 DON:** This is a clean fork of your options. If they successfully protect Kyo, just develop a Newgate. If they do not have the protection and they dropped a Linlin, instead just gloriosa it, and push 7 life. This will guarantee they go down to 3, and you can cheaply guard their next leader swing with 1k (assuming they play Shiki).   
- **8 DON:** Shiki and we leave him parked. You are likely continuing a shiki war here, where you both play them and leave them on a standoff.   
- **10 DON:** Play rocks into Shiki, and if you have space for a Kyo on the board, you can play it to cycle. However, remember you will need another one to guarantee your blockers or John will be safe buffers on the final turns. If your gloriosa is still standing, this is a good turn to attack, because your Shikis will make defense a lot more manageable, given your opponent needs to play a SEC Rocks, so will have no DON to allocate. 

In the ideal scenario, your next turn you will have Rocks 2x shiki and Kyo. And here is where you have the tempo advantage. If they did not rest their characters at all, chances are you can get them down to either 1 or 0 here, and play Stussy to stun Newgate and either Shiki or Rocks. So you get a lethal window while they are forced to swing at your board, with two of their bodies stuck standing. If you push correctly, and have another Stussy, you should be able to extend this bad situation until you win the game. 

### **Key cards**

Kyo serves as protection for your Linlins and blockers in the early game. But also excels late game to make sure you can safely set up your blockers. Try not to trash too many for counter or Leader ability. 

Chances are we will play a single Newgate, unless we are running short on Shiki. There are some good windows on both curves for him, but after 7 don, you will barely ever want to drop him over the 7 cost. 

Shiki is the key card here, and missing one is abysmal. Mid game is defined by who can safely swing with him, so pretty much always look for more copies, and never let go of him for counter, unless you have already piled up all 4 copies, and you maybe can trash one. 

Streusen is a great consistency tool, especially when going first. And after the Rocks have dropped, it will always help find more Stussys or Gloriosas. 

Once more, Stussy is the best card you have available to you in the endgame, so keep that in mind if you are forced to trash it. It is not unlikely that you end up in a game where both players chain the full playset. In these games, you do not want to be the one that ends up falling short.  

Gloriosa is a huge protagonist when going second, since you want to chain them back to back. But there are also late game spots where combined with stussy, helps handle the pressure, so there’s a big chance 3 copies are played in a single game (when it goes long). 

## **Trash effects \- When and What**

Rocks is a deck that runs at least 34 bricks, and relies heavily on character’s abilities to counter, as well as to protect the board. And to top it off, trashing is part of our leader’s ability as well. So that begs the question, when do I trash a card, and more importantly: which one do I trash. Getting this wrong can cost you games, so learning the basics is imperative to play the deck effectively. 

You need to get rid of the weaker cards you have, either in the matchup or in your curve. The first card to think about here is Linlin, which will be the easiest one to trash when we are playing on the even curve. There will be no opportunities for her before the 10 rocks, so just let it go, even if it seems like a broken card. The only exception is when you have no newgates by 6 don, and a single linlin, since she’s the best fallback there. Funnily enough, when going second, this role reverses, and newgate is who ends up left out, so you can get rid of him, as long as you can play Linlin on 5 and shiki on 7\. 

Next thing to keep in mind when trashing is the card count for each option you have. We have talked a bit about how many of each card we will want on different matchups, so try and keep a mental map of these numbers, and then count how many more are in the deck. If you have multiples of a card like Kyo, and none in trash, you can likely afford to drop them. 

For the big hitters like Shiki and Newgate, you just need to understand whether you need multiples in hand. Endgame board is Rocks, Newgate. Shiki a second copy of either, and one flex spot for either defense or protection, so that limits how many extra copies you will get to play after that. The flex spots are either blockers, stussy, Kyo or captain John So pretty much everything else can be let go from hand, unless you need to replace a piece on board. Also try and never trash counters ,as they are your most coveted resource. 

Speaking of counters, you should try to set a priority list for which ones you wanna keep in hand (so counter with the others). Authority is key, followed by SEC rocks, then Rocks Pirates event, and finally Buckin. This will change in some matchups, but treat it as the starting point. 

To illustrate the point, let’s look at a concrete example. We are swinging with leader on our 6 DON turn, What card should we get rid of?

![][image5]

You guessed it\! Here we want to get rid of Linlin\! We will not have a good window to play her, since now Newgate is better, and next turn we want to drop Shiki. Right after that SEC Rocks is mandatory, and we have a very strong combo of Newgate \+ Stussy. But even gloriosa is a more flexible tool here, since she could come up from rocks or the turn immediately after. 

### **When to use Newgate and Shiki abilities**

Newgate let’s us give \+3k to our leader for a battle, either when he attacks or is attacked, but only once per turn. The defending is easy, if they swing 7, the answer will be yes unless we really want more resources. This part will apply identically to shiki. Just defend when it is efficient or when you need to leverage your bricks in hand, because you might not do so next turn.   

Newgate on offense is a different story, we want to use it when the extra pressure to life will force a bad decision from our opponent, or when a swing at board trades 1 of our cards for 2 of theirs. And of course, when going for a lethal turn, leverage him properly. In the early game, ask yourself the next question: Do they want to take life? If they do, don’t buff the leader. This is super clear when they’re sitting at 4 life with 5 in hand, but will get a bit more complicated in most games, so just consider the fact you’re spending a card here, so it needs to be worth it. As a general rule, if taking the life or losing the character is something the opponent should avoid, push with newgate. 

Shiki follows a similar pattern, but is more predictable, because they cannot bait you by taking life when they have plenty of counters. You know whether a character is important. If you need to remove it, pitch a card, if you’re okay with it surviving, feel free to take it slow, and use that same card to protect against the counterattack. It is tempting to always trash, but remember that even you have finite resources. 

## **Leaving note**

I just wanted to thank you for reading this guide\!

 I am not the best player in the format, and this guide was not written with the intention to be the best one. It’s the first guide I write, and I just wanted to share my knowledge with the world, and test the waters to see if I enjoyed it. I have played this deck since the first day, and this was my way to share what my experience has given me. 

It has been helpful for me to articulate my thoughts, and even though some of them might not be complete, I hope they help you pick up this deck, and have as much fun with it as I have had so far. 

Thanks for reading, and I hope you enjoyed it\!
